asset-finance|healthcare-and-dental.h1: Asset finance for dental and healthcare practices
asset-finance|healthcare-and-dental.title: Asset Finance for Dental and Healthcare Practices | Loanleaf
asset-finance|healthcare-and-dental.desc: How asset finance works for dental practices, clinics and care providers buying chairs, scanners or vehicles. One short form, one specialist broker.
asset-finance|healthcare-and-dental.lead: Spread the cost of clinical equipment over its working life, with the equipment itself usually acting as the security.
intro: Clinical equipment is one of the clearer cases for asset finance. A dental chair, a cone beam scanner, a laser or a set of physio treatment couches has a known price, a known working life and a resale market, so a lender can see what it would be recovering if repayments stopped. That is why asset finance is often the first option a healthcare broker looks at for a practice that needs to replace or add equipment.

The question is usually which structure fits. Hire purchase suits kit you will use for a decade, such as surgery units and compressors. Leasing can suit technology that dates quickly, such as digital imaging software and intraoral scanners, where you may want to upgrade at the end. A broker can compare both against the expected life of what you are buying and the income it will generate. Asking for both quotes side by side shows the difference in monthly cost and tax treatment.
uses: New surgery fit-out
Equip an extra surgery with a chair, delivery unit, light, compressor and suction, financed as one package so the repayments start alongside the new patient list.
Digital imaging and scanners
Move from film or older panoramic units to digital X-ray, CBCT or intraoral scanning, often on a shorter lease so you can upgrade as the technology changes.
Autoclaves and decontamination
Replace sterilisation kit that no longer meets current standards, a purchase that cannot wait for a quiet quarter.
Vehicles for mobile care
Finance a car or van for a domiciliary care team, a mobile dental service or a community physio round.
fit: Amounts and terms

Single items run from a few thousand pounds for a scanner to well into six figures for a full surgery suite. Terms commonly follow the working life of the kit, so a chair might be financed over five to seven years and software-heavy equipment over three or four. A deposit is often requested for used or specialist items.
What lenders check about the kit

The supplier, the age and condition of used equipment, and how easily it could be resold all matter. Mainstream dental and clinical brands from established suppliers are usually easier to place than niche or older machines. A supplier quote on headed paper is normally the starting point.
What lenders check about the practice

Expect questions about trading history, whether income is mainly NHS contract or private, and who owns the practice. For larger packages, lenders may also ask about CQC registration and the make-up of the directors or partners. Clear accounts and a short note on how the new kit adds income help.
considerations: Payments run for the full term

You pay for the whole agreement even if a machine is underused or a clinician leaves. Check that the equipment will realistically pay for itself before committing, and be wary of financing capacity you cannot yet fill with patients.
Lease or buy changes the tax picture

Hire purchase and leasing are treated differently for VAT and tax relief, and capital allowances may apply to equipment you own. Your accountant should look at this before you choose a structure, as it can change the true cost.
Fit-out and building work often sit outside it

Asset finance covers the equipment, not usually the plumbing, flooring and joinery around it. If most of the cost is building work, an unsecured or secured loan may suit better, and a broker may suggest splitting the package between the two.
faqs: Can I finance second-hand dental or clinical equipment?

Often, yes, though lenders look more closely at the age, condition and supplier. Used kit from a reputable dealer with a service history is usually easier to place than a private sale. A deposit may be asked for, and the term is often shorter than for new equipment.
Is it better to lease or use hire purchase for a dental chair?

It depends on how long you plan to keep it. Hire purchase usually ends with you owning the chair, which suits long-lived kit. Leasing keeps payments lower in some cases and lets you hand equipment back, which can suit technology. Your accountant can compare the tax treatment of each.
Can asset finance cover installation and training?

Some lenders will include delivery, installation and sometimes training in the amount financed if they are itemised on the supplier’s invoice. This varies, so ask the broker early and have the supplier quote broken down into its parts. Delivery, installation and training are separate lines on many equipment quotes, so asking the supplier to itemise them early avoids delays once the application is with a lender.
Does it matter if most of my income is NHS work?

Not in itself. Lenders often see contracted NHS income as steady, but they will want to understand the contract length and value. A practice with mostly private income is assessed on patient volumes and how consistent they are. Either can be financed.
What if I want to refinance equipment I already own?

Asset refinance lets a company raise cash against equipment it owns outright, with the kit used as security. It can be useful for releasing money for a refurbishment, but you will be repaying on equipment you already have, so compare the cost carefully.

unsecured-business-loans|healthcare-and-.h1: Unsecured business loans for dental and healthcare firms
unsecured-business-loans|healthcare-and-.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Dental and Healthcare | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|healthcare-and-.desc: How unsecured business loans suit dental practices, clinics and care providers paying for a refit or new hires. Get matched with one specialist broker.
unsecured-business-loans|healthcare-and-.lead: A fixed-term loan for the parts of a practice that no lender can take away, from refits to associate hires.
intro: A lot of what a healthcare business spends on does not leave anything to repossess. Refitting a waiting area, hiring a hygienist before the diary fills, rebranding a clinic or paying for a compliance overhaul all create value for the practice, but none of it is equipment a lender could sell on. Unsecured loans are designed for this kind of spending, and they do not require you to put the building or the kit up as security.

Lenders will look at the practice rather than an asset. They will want to see steady patient income, sensible margins after clinical staff costs, and a clear reason for borrowing. Practices with a strong NHS contract or a loyal private list often present well. The trade-off is that unsecured lending is usually capped by revenue, and directors are normally asked for personal guarantees. Lenders also like to hear how any extra clinical capacity will be filled, and by whom.
uses: Hiring clinicians ahead of income
Pay a new associate, hygienist or nurse for the months it takes for their diary to fill, rather than stretching existing cash.
Cosmetic refit and rebrand
Refresh reception, treatment rooms and signage for a private-pay clinic where appearance affects patient choice.
Compliance and software upgrades
Cover a new patient records system, data security work or upgrades needed after an inspection.
Buying out a partner
Fund a partner’s retirement or exit where the amount is modest and the practice has strong trading figures.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Amounts are usually set against annual revenue, so a practice turning over £600,000 is looking at a different range to one turning over £2m. Terms commonly run from one to five years. Matching the term to how long the spending takes to earn back, such as an associate’s ramp-up, keeps repayments comfortable.
How lenders read healthcare accounts

They look at the split between NHS and private income, patient numbers, and whether the practice depends on one or two principal clinicians. A practice where income would stop if one dentist left is seen as higher risk, so a clear picture of cover and contracts helps.
Personal guarantees

Most unsecured lenders ask directors to guarantee the loan. In a practice with several partners or directors, it is worth agreeing in advance how any guarantee would be shared and what happens if someone leaves.
considerations: Cost against secured options

Without an asset behind it, an unsecured loan can cost more than finance secured on equipment or property. For a large equipment purchase, asset finance is usually the cheaper route, and a broker may suggest using the two together.
Repayments do not flex with the diary

Fixed instalments continue through holiday weeks, staff absence and a drop in private bookings. Check the repayments against your leanest months rather than your average, particularly if private income varies.
Not a long-term fix for cash gaps

If NHS or local authority payments regularly arrive late, a loan can mask a pattern that a revolving facility or better payment planning would handle more cheaply. Borrow for a project, not to cover recurring shortfalls.
faqs: Can a recently bought practice borrow on this basis?

The company needs to have traded for at least six months with revenue of £50,000 or more to be eligible for a Loanleaf introduction. Beyond that, lenders look at the practice’s track record, so a practice acquired recently with a long trading history can be viewed differently from one that is genuinely new.
Do lenders treat NHS and private income differently?

They can. Contracted NHS income is often seen as predictable, while private income is judged on patient volumes and consistency. Lenders may ask for a breakdown of both. Having it ready for the broker usually saves time. Having that split ready for the broker, along with the number of clinicians and surgeries, makes it easier to explain the practice to a lender.
What documents will I need?

Typically recent business bank statements, the latest filed accounts and sometimes management accounts. For a clinic, a summary showing the split of income by source and the number of clinicians can help the broker present the case. Having that split ready for the broker usually saves time and avoids a lender asking again later.
Will an unsecured loan affect my ability to buy premises later?

Existing borrowing is taken into account by any future lender, so repayments reduce what looks affordable. If a premises purchase is planned in the next couple of years, mention it to the broker so they can plan the order of borrowing.
What if I need a very large amount?

Unsecured lending has limits that depend on revenue and profit. If the amount needed is high relative to turnover, a broker may suggest a secured loan or a commercial mortgage, which can reach larger sums because property is offered as security.

commercial-mortgages|healthcare-and-dent.h1: Commercial mortgages for dental and healthcare practices
commercial-mortgages|healthcare-and-dent.title: Commercial Mortgages for Dental and Healthcare | Loanleaf
commercial-mortgages|healthcare-and-dent.desc: How commercial mortgages work for dental practices, clinics and care providers buying or refinancing premises. One short form, matched with a specialist broker.
commercial-mortgages|healthcare-and-dent.lead: Buy the building your practice trades from, with a mortgage assessed on the strength of the practice itself.
intro: For many practice owners, the biggest cost after clinical staff is rent. A commercial mortgage lets the company, or sometimes a separate property vehicle owned by the principals, buy the premises instead. Lenders that work with healthcare tend to look favourably at dental and medical practices because they are specialised, regulated and often have loyal patient lists that survive a change of ownership. Specialist healthcare lenders also understand that a practice’s value is tied closely to its patients.

The building matters as well as the business. A purpose-built surgery with parking, ground-floor access and rooms already plumbed for clinical use is easier to value than a converted house. Lenders will usually order a valuation that considers the property as a practice and as a general commercial unit. That second figure can limit how much they are willing to lend. Expect the valuer to ask about the layout, the number of surgeries and whether the building could be used for anything else.
uses: Buying the practice building
Move from a lease to ownership of the premises you already trade from, fixing a major cost and building equity.
Buying an existing practice with its premises
Acquire a retiring principal’s practice together with the freehold, usually with a larger deposit and some seller involvement.
Refinancing an existing mortgage
Replace an older mortgage with one that suits your current repayments, or raise extra capital against the equity built up.
A property company holding the building
Where the principals own the freehold personally or through a separate company, finance the building and lease it to the practice at a commercial rent.
fit: Loan to value and deposit

Lenders commonly lend a proportion of the lower of the purchase price or valuation, so a meaningful deposit is expected, often a quarter or more of the price. Where a practice is bought with its premises, lenders may treat goodwill separately, which can affect how much is available.
Terms and structure

Terms can stretch well beyond other business loans, often fifteen to twenty-five years, with repayment or part-interest structures available. A longer term lowers the monthly figure but increases the total interest paid, which is worth setting against the saving on rent.
What lenders look at

They review the practice’s profit and cash flow to confirm the mortgage payments would be comfortably covered, the building’s condition and use class, and any planning or CQC considerations. For a leased-back structure they also check the rent is reasonable against the market.
considerations: The building as a separate asset

A specialist building can be harder to sell if the practice closes, and lenders know it. Expect questions about alternative use and how the practice would continue if a principal left. Planning consent for clinical use should be confirmed before you commit.
Rent saved is not the whole story

Ownership brings repairs, insurance, business rates and the capital cost of keeping the premises compliant. Compare the full cost of owning against current rent, including a realistic allowance for maintenance.
Longer timescales and fees

Valuations, searches and legal work on a commercial property take time, and fees are payable on both sides. Do not leave this to the last weeks of a lease, and allow for Stamp Duty Land Tax on a purchase.
faqs: Can the practice company buy its own building?

Yes, many do, though some principals prefer a separate property company or personal ownership, sometimes through a pension arrangement. Each structure has different tax and lending consequences, so it is worth taking tax advice before choosing. Lenders will want to see which entity owns the building and which one pays the rent, and a broker can explain which structures they usually accept.
How much deposit would I normally need?

Lenders often ask for around a quarter or more of the price, although it varies by lender, property and the strength of the practice. A broker can explain what is realistic. Equity in other property or a seller’s retained interest can sometimes help.
Does the mortgage cover buying a practice as well as the building?

Sometimes. Some lenders will finance the property and a portion of the goodwill together, while others only lend against the building. Combining a commercial mortgage with a secured loan or other finance is a common approach. Where goodwill is financed, lenders usually expect the seller to stay on for a handover period, so patients are more likely to remain.
What if I rent out part of the building?

Rental income from other tenants, such as a physio or an aesthetics clinician, can count towards affordability, particularly if there are written tenancy agreements. Lenders may treat the building as part owner-occupied and part investment. Lenders will usually ask to see the leases and may adjust affordability if the tenant’s own income is uncertain or the lease is short.
Is a commercial mortgage the right choice if I may sell the practice soon?

Possibly not. Early repayment charges can apply, and a sale of the practice may complicate things if the building is held separately. If a sale is likely within a few years, discuss it with the broker before committing. A sale of the building and a sale of the practice can also be handled separately, so ask how a buyer would take on the loan.

secured-business-loans|healthcare-and-de.h1: Secured business loans for healthcare and dental firms
secured-business-loans|healthcare-and-de.title: Secured Business Loans for Healthcare and Dental | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|healthcare-and-de.desc: How secured business loans help dental practices and clinics buy another practice, buy out partners or raise larger sums against property. Free to use.
secured-business-loans|healthcare-and-de.lead: Larger sums for a practice acquisition or buy-out, secured against property or other assets the business owns.
intro: Secured loans come into their own when the amount is more than a practice’s revenue alone would support. Buying a second dental practice, buying out a partner or consolidating several older facilities all involve sums that unsecured lenders tend to cap. Offering security, usually property owned by the company or its directors, widens the options and can bring longer terms and a lower cost. That is why rented practices often need to look at a different route.

For healthcare firms the security question is rarely straightforward. Many practices rent, so there may be no building to charge. Directors might offer a personal property instead, which brings a different level of risk. Some lenders will take a debenture over the company’s assets, but clinical equipment and goodwill are harder to value than a freehold. A broker will look at which of these lenders accept. Ask early which of these your own situation supports.
uses: Acquiring a second practice
Pay for a competing or neighbouring practice, with the price often split between a secured loan, seller finance and your own cash.
Buying out a retiring partner
Fund a partner’s share where the business is sound but the amount is too large for an unsecured loan.
Consolidating older borrowing
Combine several loans, leases and overdrafts into one secured loan with a single monthly payment, often over a longer term.
Raising money against owned premises
Release equity from a building the practice owns to fund a refurbishment or additional surgeries.
fit: Amounts and what they depend on

The loan is usually a share of the value of the security, so the equity in the property matters more than the practice’s turnover. Acquisition sizes in dentistry can reach seven figures, and lenders may combine property security with a charge over the company.
Valuing a practice as security

Lenders can be cautious about goodwill because it depends on patients staying after a handover. Where the loan funds an acquisition, expect them to look at the vendor’s accounts, patient numbers and the treatment mix, and to ask how much time the seller will stay on.
Personal property as security

If a director’s home or investment property is offered, independent legal advice is often required, and the risk is personal. A broker can explain which lenders accept it and what the alternatives might be, such as a larger deposit.
considerations: Risk to the asset offered

If the practice cannot repay, the lender can act against the property. That includes a director’s home where it has been offered. Only offer security you are comfortable putting at risk, and take independent advice.
Valuation and legal costs
Valuation fees, legal fees on both sides and arrangement fees add up and are often payable even if the deal does not complete. Ask for a full list of costs before instructing anyone.
Time to complete
Charges must be registered and due diligence carried out on any practice being bought. Allow for several weeks at least, longer if consent from an existing lender or a landlord is needed.
faqs: What security can a practice that rents its premises offer?

Options include a debenture over company assets, property owned by the directors, or a charge over other business assets. Lenders vary in what they accept, so tell the broker early what is available. A broker can explain which lenders accept each type, and what valuation they would need for the asset.
Can I borrow to buy another dental practice?

Yes, this is a common use. The lender will look at the practice being bought as well as your own, including its accounts, patient numbers and how it is likely to perform after the handover. Some deposit from you is usually expected.
Is a secured loan cheaper than an unsecured loan?

It can be, because the lender has something to fall back on. But valuation, legal and arrangement fees add to the cost, so for a smaller sum the unsecured route may be comparable. Look at the total repayable. A valuation and any legal work will also be needed before a lender confirms how much is available.
Will I still have to give a personal guarantee?

Sometimes. Some lenders ask for a guarantee as well as security, particularly where the security does not cover the whole loan. A broker can tell you what each lender is likely to require. Allow extra time if a landlord’s consent or a release from an older lender is needed, as these steps are often outside your control.
What happens if the practice needs to be sold during the loan?

The lender’s charge normally has to be repaid from the proceeds, or an agreed substitute security put in place. Early repayment terms vary, so check them before you sign, especially if a sale is possible. Telling the broker about any planned sale or retirement at the start lets them favour lenders with flexible early repayment terms.

merchant-cash-advance|healthcare-and-den.h1: Merchant cash advances for private clinics and practices
merchant-cash-advance|healthcare-and-den.title: Merchant Cash Advances for Private Clinics | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|healthcare-and-den.desc: When a merchant cash advance suits private clinics and practices that take card payments, and when it does not. One short form, one specialist broker.
merchant-cash-advance|healthcare-and-den.lead: A share of future card takings repays the advance, which suits private-pay clinics better than NHS-funded practices.
intro: A merchant cash advance is repaid from card sales, so it only makes sense for a healthcare business that takes a steady flow of card payments. That points mainly to private dental practices, aesthetics and cosmetic clinics, physiotherapists, opticians and other clinics where patients pay at the time of treatment. It is a poor fit for a practice whose income is mostly NHS contract payments, which arrive by bank transfer.

Providers look at the history of card takings through your terminal rather than at the practice’s assets. This can make it quicker to arrange than a loan and available to a clinic with little to offer as security, such as one operating from rented premises. Because repayments follow takings, they ease off in the quieter weeks around holidays, which is where it differs most from a fixed-term loan. That suits private income that rises and falls with the season.
uses: Cosmetic treatment room
Equip and open a new treatment room for teeth whitening, aligners or aesthetics, repaid from the takings those treatments bring in.
Marketing a private list
Pay for a local campaign to build private patient numbers where your income is mainly card-based.
Covering a summer dip
Smooth costs through the months when private bookings drop, such as August and the weeks around Christmas.
Rapid replacement of equipment
Replace a failed piece of kit quickly where a delay would mean cancelling appointments and the item does not suit asset finance.
fit: Which practices suit it

Clinics with consistent monthly card volume and a significant private income share. Providers usually ask how long you have taken cards, the average monthly total and who your card processor is. A practice taking mostly NHS payments will find the card history too small to support an advance.
How repayment works in practice

A fixed percentage of each card payment is taken until the agreed total is repaid. If takings are low in a given week, less is taken. If they surge, the advance clears faster. The cost is set as a fixed fee at the start, not as interest that falls with time.
Size and cost relative to the alternatives

Amounts are usually linked to monthly card takings, so they tend to be smaller than a bank or asset-backed loan. Because the fee is fixed and the advance can clear quickly, the effective annual cost can be high, so compare it with other options.
considerations: Often more expensive than a loan

When the fee is converted into an annual rate it can be much higher than a term loan, especially if you repay faster than expected. Ask the broker for the total repayable and what happens if you clear it early.
Less cash from every card payment
A slice of each card sale goes to the provider until the advance is repaid. If your margins are tight or you carry large lab bills and consumables, check that what remains still covers costs.
Light regulation

Merchant cash advances to companies are generally not regulated by the FCA, so some consumer-style protections do not apply. Read the agreement carefully, and consider whether a term loan or asset finance would suit better first.
faqs: Can I get one if most of my income is NHS payments?

Probably not in a useful amount. The product is assessed on card takings, and NHS income is paid by bank transfer. A practice with a mix may find the card share too small. Other finance, such as a term loan, will usually be more suitable.
Do patient payment plans count as card takings?

It depends on how they are taken. Payments made through your card terminal usually count. Third-party finance paid to you in a lump sum by a lender may be treated differently. The provider will tell you what it counts. The provider can tell you which types of payment it counts before you agree, and a short summary from your terminal provider usually settles it.
Is it a good way to buy a dental chair?

Usually not. Asset finance spreads the cost over several years and uses the chair as security, which is normally cheaper. A merchant cash advance is better kept for situations where speed matters or the item cannot be financed another way.
What happens if card takings fall sharply?

The amount taken falls too, so you repay more slowly. Providers can include minimum repayment terms or review clauses, so read these. A sharp drop in takings may also affect any provider’s willingness to offer a further advance. Check the agreement for minimum weekly amounts, and ask what happens if takings stay low for several months in a row.
Can I change my card terminal provider while repaying?

Often it is restricted, because repayments are taken through the terminal. Some providers use a fixed daily debit instead. Check the agreement before agreeing, particularly if you plan to switch processors or add online payment. Ask whether any early settlement discount is offered and what the provider would still expect you to pay.

revolving-credit-facility|ecommerce.h1: Revolving credit facilities for ecommerce businesses
revolving-credit-facility|ecommerce.title: Revolving Credit Facilities for Ecommerce | Loanleaf
revolving-credit-facility|ecommerce.desc: How a revolving credit facility helps online retailers buy stock before peak season and cover marketplace payout gaps. One short form, one specialist broker.
revolving-credit-facility|ecommerce.lead: A credit limit you draw on when a stock order falls due and repay as sales come in, paying interest only on what you use.
intro: Online retail runs on a repeating cycle: pay the supplier, wait for goods, sell them, wait for the payout. A revolving credit facility fits that cycle closely. You draw on the limit to pay a supplier deposit, repay as customer orders clear, then draw again for the next order. Interest is charged only on the amount drawn, so a limit that sits unused through January costs little beyond any commitment fees.

It is most useful for sellers whose stock needs are lumpy. A brand that buys three big batches a year from a manufacturer abroad does not need a fixed loan running all twelve months. It needs cash at the moment of ordering and again at the freight stage. Lenders will want to see that sales are consistent enough for the facility to clear regularly rather than become a standing debt.
uses: Supplier deposits
Pay the 30% to 50% deposit many overseas manufacturers ask for at order, then repay as the goods arrive and sell.
Peak season build
Fund the extra stock and fulfilment capacity for Black Friday and Christmas, and repay in January when the sales have cleared.
Bridging marketplace payouts
Cover costs while Amazon or another marketplace holds back payouts, such as reserves taken after a spike in returns.
Freight and duty on arrival
Pay shipping, customs duty and import VAT when containers land, before the goods are ready to sell.
fit: How limits are usually set

Lenders often base the limit on a share of recent monthly revenue, sometimes with a view of stock value. Facilities may be agreed for twelve months and reviewed at renewal. Limits suit sellers with sales that are steady enough to show repeated drawing and repaying.
Seeing sales data

Many lenders working with online businesses ask to connect to your store, payment provider or marketplace account and read live sales and refund figures. Clean reporting, consistent refund rates and a clear gross margin by product make it easier to set an appropriate limit.
Matching drawdowns to the stock cycle

A facility works best when each drawing has a clear repayment date, such as the sell-through period for a batch. Many brands plan to clear the limit fully at least once a year. A limit that never clears signals to lenders, and to you, that the borrowing has become permanent.
considerations: Fees beyond interest
There may be arrangement, renewal and unused-limit fees. For a business that draws rarely, these can be a large share of the total cost. Ask for a worked example based on your own order pattern.
Limits can be reviewed or withdrawn
A bad quarter, a rise in returns or a change in the sales channel mix can lead a lender to reduce the limit at review. Do not rely on the facility as the only source of cash for a major order.
Not suited to long-term investment

A warehouse fit-out or a lengthy product development is not a good use. Those need a fixed term loan so repayments are planned. A broker may suggest combining a term loan for the project with a facility for stock.
faqs: How is a revolving facility different from a business overdraft?

A facility is usually a separate account arranged with a specialist lender, often with a clearer limit and review date, and may not be tied to your bank. An overdraft is attached to your current account and can be withdrawn on demand. A broker can compare both for you.
Can I draw on it immediately for a supplier payment?

Once the facility is agreed, drawdowns are usually quick, often within a working day, but each lender sets its own process. It is best to have the facility in place before you need to place a big order, not while waiting to pay.
Will a lender want security over my stock?

Some do. A debenture or a charge over stock can be requested, and some lenders will also ask for a personal guarantee from directors. Others offer unsecured facilities with a lower limit. The broker will explain what each lender asks.
Does the facility work for dropshippers?

It can, though lenders will look at how your cash cycle works. A dropshipper that pays the supplier after the customer pays needs less working capital than a stockholder, so the facility may be smaller or less suited. Margins and ad spend usually decide the need.
What if I sell on several marketplaces and my own site?

Lenders generally welcome a mix, since it spreads risk, but they will want sales data from each. Being able to show revenue by channel and your refund rate for each makes the application easier to assess. Having a short channel-by-channel summary ready for the broker avoids repeated requests from lenders.

unsecured-business-loans|ecommerce.h1: Unsecured business loans for ecommerce companies
unsecured-business-loans|ecommerce.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Ecommerce Companies | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|ecommerce.desc: How unsecured business loans suit online retailers paying for a warehouse move, a product range or a paid advertising push. Matched with one specialist broker.
unsecured-business-loans|ecommerce.lead: A fixed loan for one-off projects in an online business, from a new range to a bigger unit, with no stock or property as security.
intro: An online business often has very little to put up as security. Stock turns over quickly, the premises may be rented, and the main asset is a brand and a customer list that no lender can easily value. Unsecured loans are built for this position. They are assessed on the trading record, the accounts and the sales data, which an ecommerce company can usually show in far more detail than a high street shop.

The best uses are specific projects with an end date and a measurable return: a new product range, a move into a larger fulfilment unit, a launch in a new market. They suit less well as a way to keep a stock cycle going month after month, where a revolving facility fits better. Repayments are fixed, so they need to be affordable in a slow January as well as a busy November.
uses: Launching a new range
Pay for design, samples, tooling and the first production run of a new product line, then repay as it sells.
Moving to a bigger unit
Fund the deposit, racking, packing stations and fit-out for a larger warehouse or fulfilment space.
Entering a new market
Cover localised sites, translated listings, compliance testing and the first shipment for sales in the EU or the US.
Brand and creative investment
Invest in photography, a rebuilt storefront or a retention programme that will pay back over a longer horizon than a single campaign.
fit: Amounts and terms

Loan size is typically linked to annual revenue and profit, with terms from one to five years. A seller turning over £800,000 and showing steady margins may qualify for a very different amount to one whose revenue has swung. Shorter terms suit projects with a quick payback.
Reading ecommerce accounts

Lenders look at gross margin after advertising costs, the refund rate, and how much revenue comes from repeat customers. A business where growth has depended on rising ad spend that now returns less will be viewed more cautiously than one with a stable base of returning buyers.
Directors’ guarantees

Most unsecured lenders ask for personal guarantees. For an online seller with no assets to fall back on, this is common, so understand what you are signing and how it would operate if the company struggled.
considerations: Repayments against uneven revenue

Sales that peak in Q4 and fall back afterwards make fixed instalments harder to manage. Test the monthly payment against your weakest three months, and think about whether a seasonal repayment plan is available.
A project that may not repay itself
A new range can take longer to sell through than planned, and returns eat into margin. Build in a cushion, and be realistic about the time before the investment starts to pay for itself.
Cost compared with revenue-based options

Revenue-based finance repays as you sell, but can cost more overall. A term loan is usually cheaper if you are confident of repaying it on schedule. The right answer depends on how predictable your sales are.
faqs: Can I use an unsecured loan to pay for advertising?

Yes, though lenders look closely at whether advertising spend has produced profitable sales in the past. If your return on ad spend has been consistent, lenders may be more comfortable. A loan for ads alone suits less well than one for a project with lasting value.
Do lenders need to see my Shopify or Amazon data?

Many lenders working with online businesses ask for read-only access to your store or marketplace account, or to export reports. It lets them check sales, refunds and trends directly. Bank statements and filed accounts are still normally required. A lender will often want a wider picture as well, such as a breakdown of revenue by channel.
Is a dropshipping business eligible?

A company trading for six months or more, with revenue over £50,000, can be matched. Lenders may be more cautious about businesses with thin margins and heavy ad dependence, so having clear figures on profit after advertising is helpful. Exports from your store and ad accounts can fill gaps if a lender is not able to connect directly.
What if my accounts show a loss because I invested in growth?

A loss can limit the options, but lenders will look at the reason for it. A business reinvesting heavily with strong gross margins and revenue growth is viewed differently from one losing money on each sale. Management accounts can help explain the position.
How quickly can the money arrive?

It varies by lender and how quickly you supply documents. Some can decide within a few days, others take longer for larger amounts. Having bank statements, accounts and sales exports ready usually speeds things up. No timescale can be promised.

merchant-cash-advance|ecommerce.h1: Merchant cash advances and revenue-based finance online
merchant-cash-advance|ecommerce.title: Merchant Cash Advances for Ecommerce Sellers | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|ecommerce.desc: How revenue-based finance and merchant cash advances work for online sellers on Shopify, Amazon and card platforms, and when a loan may suit better.
merchant-cash-advance|ecommerce.lead: Repayments taken as a share of your online sales, so they rise and fall with the orders you actually receive.
intro: For online sellers, the card-takings advance has a close relative: revenue-based finance. Instead of reading the card terminal in a shop, the provider connects to your Shopify store, Stripe or PayPal account, or marketplace seller account, and reads your sales. The advance is then repaid as a fixed percentage of daily or weekly revenue, until the total is cleared. In a slow week, less is taken. Daily or weekly sales are usually the figure that sets the amount and the repayment.

That flexibility is the appeal for a seller with unpredictable sales, a short trading record or no assets. Some providers will decide using sales data alone. The cost, however, is usually a fixed fee set at the outset, and it can be high compared with a term loan when the advance clears quickly. It tends to work best for short, high-return uses, such as stock for a proven bestseller. Check the total repayable before comparing it with other products.
uses: Stock for a proven bestseller
Reorder a product that has repeatedly sold through, where you are confident the extra stock will clear within a few weeks.
A time-limited ad push
Spend more on advertising around a sales event where you can see from previous years how sales respond.
Covering a marketplace reserve
Replace cash held back by a marketplace after a spike in returns or a policy review, until payouts catch up.
Seasonal pre-order costs
Pay suppliers early to secure stock and better terms for the busiest part of the year.
fit: Data providers usually want to see

Most ask for read access to your store and payment accounts, plus a few months of statements. They look at monthly revenue, how steady it is, the refund and chargeback rate, and the mix between direct sales and marketplaces.
How repayment tracks sales

A fixed percentage of each day’s or week’s revenue goes to the provider until the total is cleared. If you sell more, it clears sooner. This protects cash in a slow month, but it also means a good month repays at a faster pace than you may have planned for.
Where it sits among the options

Amounts are usually a multiple of monthly revenue, so they tend to be modest. It generally suits a business that needs speed and flexibility more than the lowest cost. For a planned project with predictable income, a term loan is usually cheaper.
considerations: Check the true cost

Because the cost is a flat fee, a quick repayment makes the effective annual rate higher. Ask for the total repayable, and what happens if you repay early. Compare it with a term loan or a revolving facility.
Dependence on your sales platform

Repayments are linked to the accounts that provider reads. Changing payment processor, moving sales to another platform or adding a new channel can affect repayment. Check what the agreement requires if you do.
Cash margin after repayment
If advertising, shipping and product costs are high, handing over a fixed share of revenue could leave little. Run the numbers on net cash, not gross sales, before agreeing.
faqs: What is the difference between this and a business loan?

A loan has fixed instalments over a set term. A revenue-based advance repays as a percentage of your sales, so payments vary and the term depends on how quickly you sell. The cost is usually a fixed fee, not interest. Each suits different situations.
Can I get revenue-based finance if I sell on Amazon?

Some providers connect to marketplace seller accounts and base the amount on your payouts. Others require your own store or card processing too. Which accounts they accept varies, so a broker can point you to those who work with your channel.
Will it affect my ability to get a bank loan later?

It is a commitment other lenders will see on your statements and in your accounts. It may reduce what they consider affordable, particularly while it is being repaid. Mention it to the broker if you may need other finance soon.
Is the cost regulated by the FCA?

Advances to limited companies are generally not regulated by the FCA, so some protections available for other credit may not apply. Read the contract, ask for the total payable in pounds, and compare it with other options. Ask the broker to put the total repayable and the effective cost in writing so you can compare it with a loan.
What happens in a month with very few sales?

The amount taken falls with your sales, which helps cash flow. Some agreements include minimum payments or a reconciliation clause, so check. A long run of very low sales may also make the provider review the arrangement. Agreements also differ on how they treat a long stretch of low sales, so read the clause on minimum payments carefully.

vat-and-tax-loans|ecommerce.h1: VAT and tax loans for ecommerce companies
vat-and-tax-loans|ecommerce.title: VAT and Tax Loans for Ecommerce Companies | Loanleaf
vat-and-tax-loans|ecommerce.desc: How VAT and tax loans help online sellers spread import VAT, quarterly VAT and corporation tax bills, and when HMRC’s Time to Pay may be worth comparing.
vat-and-tax-loans|ecommerce.lead: Spread a large VAT, import or corporation tax bill across a set number of months instead of paying it in one go.
intro: VAT is a bigger cash event for an online seller than for most businesses. A company that imports stock pays import VAT and duty at the border, often reclaiming it later on the VAT return. A fast-growing seller then faces a quarterly return in which the VAT collected on strong sales is due just as stock is being bought for the next peak. Even a profitable business can find that cash is tied up in inventory when the bill lands.

A VAT or tax loan covers a bill that has a firm date and a known amount. It is usually repaid in fixed instalments over a few months up to around a year. It suits a company that is trading well but has its cash committed to stock and advertising. It is not a way to bridge repeated shortfalls, and it is worth comparing the cost with HMRC’s Time to Pay.
uses: Quarterly VAT after a strong quarter
Pay a large return that follows a big Black Friday and Christmas run, while cash is tied up in January stock orders.
Import VAT and duty on a container
Cover VAT and customs charges due when a large shipment lands, where postponed accounting is not in use or cash is tight.
Corporation tax after a profitable year
Spread a corporation tax payment that falls due before the cash from the year’s trading is available.
PAYE and National Insurance on a seasonal workforce
Handle payroll taxes after taking on extra staff for peak, when the sales income has gone on stock.
fit: Amounts and terms

Loans are typically sized to the bill, and the term runs a few months to around a year, so instalments land before the next one is due. A seller with a £60,000 quarterly VAT bill might spread it over six or nine months, rather than carrying it into the following return.
Why timing matters for sellers

A lender needs time to assess the application, and the bill has a hard deadline. Plan around the return date, not the day before it. Sellers who watch the sales calendar can often see a large VAT bill coming weeks ahead and apply early.
What lenders check

They look at filed accounts, VAT returns, recent bank statements and the profitability behind the sales. A seller whose VAT is large because revenue is high, with healthy margins, is viewed differently from one where returns and ad costs are eating the profit.
considerations: Compare with HMRC Time to Pay

HMRC may agree to spread a bill, though interest is still charged and terms are not guaranteed. A tax loan costs money but means you pay HMRC in full and on time. Weigh the two, and take advice from your accountant.
Late payment penalties and interest
Paying late brings HMRC penalties and interest, which is the main reason to consider a loan. Do not let the bill become overdue while you arrange finance, as arrears can limit the lenders available.
A one-off bill, not a pattern

If VAT keeps outpacing cash, look at the underlying issue, such as stock cycle, payment terms or margin. A revolving facility or planning VAT payments separately may be cheaper than repeated tax loans.
faqs: Does postponed VAT accounting remove the need for a tax loan?

It can ease the cash impact of import VAT, because it is accounted for on your return rather than paid at the border. Quarterly VAT can still be large, though, so a loan may remain useful. Your accountant can advise on which scheme suits you.
Can the loan be paid directly to HMRC?

Some lenders pay HMRC directly, and others pay the money into your account for you to settle the bill. Either way, you are responsible for making the payment on time. Ask the broker how each lender handles it. Ask the broker whether payment goes straight to HMRC or to you, and check that your own accounts team knows which.
What if my VAT bill is already overdue?

Existing arrears limit the options, and some lenders will not consider an application. If you are in this position, tell the broker at once. They may be able to suggest alternatives, and contacting HMRC about a payment arrangement may also be worth doing.
Should I use a loan or stagger my stock orders?

It depends on margin and timing. Staggering stock may reduce the VAT impact but could cost more in freight or lose supplier discounts. Your accountant can model the cost of each path. Stock decisions also affect margin and customer service, so the cheapest tax path is not always the best choice for the business.
Is a loan to pay tax allowed to be unsecured?

Most tax loans are unsecured, though a lender may ask for a personal guarantee from the directors. The amount offered usually depends on the size of the bill and the company’s trading strength. Your broker will explain what each lender requires.

invoice-finance|ecommerce.h1: Invoice finance for ecommerce businesses with trade sales
invoice-finance|ecommerce.title: Invoice Finance for Ecommerce With Trade Sales | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|ecommerce.desc: When invoice finance works for online sellers that also supply retailers, wholesale accounts or corporate buyers on credit terms, and when it does not apply.
invoice-finance|ecommerce.lead: Invoice finance only applies to the part of an online business that invoices other companies on credit terms.
intro: Most online sales are paid for at the checkout, so there is no invoice to borrow against. That makes invoice finance a narrow fit for ecommerce. It becomes relevant when a brand also sells to other businesses: a wholesale account with a high street chain, a corporate gifting contract, a supply deal with a retailer, or a B2B portal where customers order on 30 or 60 day terms. Then there is a real sales ledger.

A growing number of direct-to-consumer brands find that their trade channel brings in large orders but slower cash. A retailer may order £50,000 of stock and pay 60 days after delivery, while the brand pays its manufacturer up front. Invoice finance releases most of that value soon after the invoice is raised. The consumer side of the business stays outside it, and a broker may suggest a different product for that part.
uses: Wholesale accounts to retailers
Release the value of invoices from stockists and department stores that settle in 45 to 90 days.
Corporate and promotional orders
Finance large one-off corporate orders where the customer pays on terms after delivery.
A new trade channel
Build a wholesale arm without starving the direct sales side of cash as the invoices work through.
Subscription or box supply to businesses
Where you invoice other companies monthly for supply, release the cash each month as invoices are raised.
fit: Which invoices count

Providers fund invoices to other businesses, not consumer orders. Marketplace payouts are usually not accepted as invoices. Your wholesale ledger needs to be large enough and spread across customers, and the buyers need to be creditworthy.
Typical structure

A provider advances a large share of each approved invoice, often up to around 80 to 90%, and pays the balance, less fees, when your customer pays. Some lenders will finance only selected invoices from the trade side rather than the whole business.
Customer concentration

If one retail chain makes up most of your trade sales, lenders will look hard at that customer’s payment record and may set a limit on how much they will advance against it. A broader spread of trade customers makes the facility simpler to arrange.
considerations: Often a small fit for a mainly online seller

If trade is only a small share of revenue, the sales ledger may not meet a provider’s minimum, and fixed charges can outweigh the benefit. For consumer-heavy sellers, a revolving facility or unsecured loan is usually more suitable.
Fees and notice periods

Providers charge a service fee and a discount on the money advanced, and contracts often include minimum terms and notice periods. Check that the cost of financing the invoices is still sensible against the margin on trade orders, which are often lower than direct sales.
Retailer terms and chargebacks

Retailers may deduct returns, marketing contributions or late-delivery penalties from an invoice. Lenders will want to know how often this happens, because it reduces what they can recover. Keep records of deductions by customer.
faqs: Can I use invoice finance on consumer orders or marketplace payouts?

Generally not. Invoice finance relies on invoices to other businesses on credit terms. Consumer orders are paid at purchase, and marketplace payouts are not normally treated as invoices. Other products, such as a revolving facility, suit that side better. A broker can tell you whether any part of your sales is suitable, such as a wholesale arm or a corporate account.
Does my customer need to know I am using it?

With factoring, the provider collects payment and customers know. With invoice discounting you manage collections and customers are often unaware. Which one is available depends on the size of your business and the provider. Providers differ on how they handle disclosure, so ask in advance if confidentiality matters to your trade customers.
Can I finance just some invoices?

Some providers offer selective or spot facilities for single invoices or customers, which can suit a seller with only occasional trade sales. They tend to cost more per invoice than a full facility, so compare what suits your volumes. A broker can tell you which providers offer this, and how the minimum charges compare with those on a full facility.
What if my retail customer pays late?

Late payment extends the time the advance is outstanding, and the discount charge grows. Some agreements include a limit on how long an invoice can remain unpaid before it is removed from the facility. Check the terms and how recourse works.
Is it worth it for a small wholesale arm?

It can be if the invoices are large and the payment terms long, but providers often set minimums and charge fixed fees. A broker can say whether your ledger is likely to be large enough, or whether another product suits better.

unsecured-business-loans|professional-se.h1: Unsecured business loans for professional services firms
unsecured-business-loans|professional-se.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Professional Services | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|professional-se.desc: How unsecured loans help accountants, architects, consultants and agencies hire ahead of income or buy a practice, with no property offered as security.
unsecured-business-loans|professional-se.lead: A fixed loan that lets a firm hire, move or acquire ahead of the fees, without putting any property or equipment on the line.
intro: A professional firm’s main asset walks out of the door each evening. There is rarely a warehouse of stock or a fleet of vehicles to charge against, which is why unsecured loans are the usual route. They are assessed on the firm’s fee income, its margins and the people paying it. A firm with long-standing clients and a steady billing record has more to show a lender than a lengthy asset register.

Timing is the main reason to borrow. A partner hired in January may not bring in a full year’s fees until the following winter. A second office costs rent and fit-out months before it earns. A loan lets the firm absorb that gap without squeezing monthly cash. Lenders will want to know how revenue is spread between clients, and how much of it would be at risk if a senior person left.
uses: Hiring a fee earner ahead of work
Pay a new associate, manager or specialist for the months before their billing covers their cost.
Opening a second office
Cover the deposit, fit-out and early running costs of a new location in a city where you already have clients.
Buying a client book or small firm
Fund the purchase of a retiring practitioner’s clients or a smaller competitor, often with deferred payments to the seller.
Technology and systems
Invest in practice management, case or project software, or secure data systems that improve billing and compliance.
fit: Amounts and terms

Lenders usually size the loan against annual revenue and profit, over terms of one to five years. A firm turning over £1.2m with steady margins will see a different range from one turning over £300,000. Matching the term to the payback period of a hire keeps repayments proportionate.
What strengthens an application

Retainers, recurring contracts and a low reliance on any one client. Lenders may ask for the largest clients by share of fees, how long they have been with the firm, and how work in progress is billed. A clear billing history makes the picture easier to read.
Guarantees and structure

Most lenders ask directors or members to give personal guarantees. In an LLP, lenders want to know who the members are and how profits are shared, so agree in advance who would stand behind the loan and how that is documented.
considerations: Revenue can leave with one person
If a firm’s fees depend on one rainmaker, lenders will treat the loan as riskier. Show how work is shared across the team, and consider whether key person cover is in place.
Fixed repayments against uneven billing
Fee income can be lumpy, with milestone billing and year-end peaks. Check that instalments can be met in your slowest quarter, not just on the average, and keep some headroom.
Partners’ drawings count

In partnerships and LLPs, lenders often consider members’ drawings when assessing affordability. Heavy drawings reduce the cash available to repay, so lenders may want to see what would continue after the loan starts.
faqs: Can an LLP take an unsecured business loan?

Yes. LLPs are eligible if they have traded for at least six months and meet the revenue threshold. Lenders will want to see the members’ agreement, how profit is shared and who would give any personal guarantees. Lenders ask whether any one client accounts for a large share of fees, and a short breakdown makes that easy to answer.
Do I need to offer my own property as security?

Not for an unsecured loan, but lenders commonly ask for a personal guarantee, which makes the directors liable if the firm cannot repay. A broker can explain how that works and which lenders ask for it. Some also accept a smaller guarantee, or one shared among several members, so ask the broker what options are available.
Will lenders look at my work in progress?

They may. Work in progress and unbilled time show how much income is on its way, so some lenders ask about it, especially for firms with project-based billing. A short summary alongside your accounts can help. A short schedule of work in progress by client, dated and valued, is normally enough, and your accountant can prepare it.
Is it a good way to buy another firm?

It can work for smaller acquisitions, often alongside seller deferral and your own money. Larger purchases may need a secured loan. Lenders will want to see the target’s accounts and how clients would be retained after the transfer. Seller deferral, where part of the price is paid over time from future fees, is common and can reduce the amount you need to borrow upfront.
How do I know how much I can borrow?

It depends mainly on revenue, profit and existing commitments, and lenders differ. A broker can give a realistic range for a firm of your size and sector. Loanleaf handles requests from £5,000 upwards. A broker can discuss your accounts and plans in more detail, and no figure can be promised until a lender has reviewed your documents.

vat-and-tax-loans|professional-services.h1: VAT and tax loans for accountancy and professional firms
vat-and-tax-loans|professional-services.title: VAT and Tax Loans for Professional Services Firms | Loanleaf
vat-and-tax-loans|professional-services.desc: How VAT and tax loans help professional services firms spread corporation tax, VAT and PAYE bills when fee income and tax deadlines do not line up.
vat-and-tax-loans|professional-services.lead: Spread a corporation tax, VAT or PAYE bill over several months when fees and the tax calendar do not line up.
intro: A professional firm can have a good year and still struggle to pay the tax on it. Fees are billed in arrears, work in progress sits on the balance sheet as an asset rather than cash, and a profitable year brings a corporation tax bill nine months after year end. Add VAT on invoices that clients have not yet paid, and the firm can owe HMRC for income it has not collected.

A VAT or tax loan puts the bill in instalments, normally over a few months up to around a year. It suits a firm that is solid but short of cash on a specific date, such as an architectural practice that billed a large stage in March and has VAT to pay in April, while the client pays in June. It is worth comparing with HMRC’s Time to Pay before applying.
uses: VAT on invoices not yet collected
Pay output VAT on billed fees while the client’s payment is still outstanding, where the firm is not on cash accounting.
Corporation tax after a strong year
Spread the payment due nine months after year end, when cash has already been spent on salaries and bonuses.
Payroll taxes after a bonus round
Cover PAYE and National Insurance triggered by year-end bonuses or new hires before the related fees are billed.
Partner or director tax
For an LLP, support members who need to settle personal tax on profits that were retained in the firm.
fit: Amounts and terms

The loan is typically sized to the bill, repaid over three to twelve months so that it is cleared before the next large payment. A firm with a £90,000 corporation tax bill might spread it across nine months, while staying ahead of the next VAT quarter.
Timing of fees against the tax date

Lenders will look at when the firm expects to collect the fees that created the bill. A bill that follows invoiced work with a clear payment date is easier to assess than one caused by an unexplained drop in cash. A short note on expected collections helps.
What lenders look at

Recent filed accounts, VAT returns, bank statements and the profit figure behind the bill. They will ask whether the firm has any HMRC arrears, and for LLPs how members’ tax is handled. Directors are often asked for a personal guarantee.
considerations: Time to Pay may cost less

HMRC may agree an arrangement, although it charges interest and agreement is not certain. A tax loan costs more in fees and interest, but it means the bill is paid on time. Ask your accountant to compare the two.
Do not borrow for the same bill every year
If tax bills keep catching the firm short, set aside funds as work is billed, or review payment terms and billing frequency. Repeated loans can add cost without fixing the cause.
Partners’ personal tax is separate
In an LLP, income tax is a personal liability of each member. Company finance generally does not cover it unless structured that way, so check which bills the loan can be used for.
faqs: Can an accountancy firm take a tax loan?

Yes. Any eligible limited company or LLP with a tax bill can apply. Lenders see the firm’s own accounts and cash flow in the same way as for other sectors, although the firm’s knowledge of its own tax position helps the application.
How far ahead should I apply?

Lenders need time to assess the application and arrange payment, so apply well before the deadline, ideally several weeks. Late payment brings HMRC interest and penalties, and arrears can reduce the number of lenders willing to consider you. Ask the broker how long each lender typically needs, and remember that your own accountant can confirm the exact bill and deadline.
Does the loan cover the VAT on invoices that clients have not paid?

It can pay the VAT bill itself regardless of whether clients have paid. If your firm regularly pays VAT before collecting it, consider cash accounting where eligible, or invoice finance to even out the gap. A broker can explain the options.
Is this the same as a Time to Pay arrangement?

No. Time to Pay is an agreement with HMRC to pay in instalments, with interest. A tax loan is borrowing from a lender, who pays or funds the bill so that HMRC is paid in full. The cost and conditions of each differ.
Can a loan cover both VAT and corporation tax together?

Some lenders will combine several tax liabilities into one loan, subject to an overall amount and affordability. Lenders may want to see the bills and due dates. A broker can tell you which lenders are likely to consider a combined request.

invoice-finance|professional-services.h1: Invoice finance for professional services firms
invoice-finance|professional-services.title: Invoice Finance for Professional Services Firms | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|professional-services.desc: How invoice finance works for consultancies, agencies and recruiters billing clients on 30 to 60 day terms, and when milestone billing makes it a poor fit.
invoice-finance|professional-services.lead: Release cash from client invoices raised for completed work, rather than waiting 30, 60 or 90 days for clients to pay.
intro: Professional firms pay their people monthly and bill their clients later. A consultancy with twenty staff has a payroll to meet before the invoice for the month’s work is even approved, and a large client may take sixty days to pay it. Invoice finance borrows against those raised invoices, so a high share of the value is advanced soon after billing, and the balance, less fees, is paid when the client settles.

It is most useful for firms with a regular flow of invoices to business clients: consultancies, marketing and creative agencies, recruitment firms, IT services and engineering practices. It is a poorer fit for firms that bill by fixed milestone or in advance, or that receive fees from consumers. Providers will look at the quality of your clients as much as at your own accounts, because the clients’ payment record underpins the facility.
uses: Covering payroll between invoice and payment
Advance cash on a month’s billing so salaries and contractor payments are not waiting on a client’s approval cycle.
Agencies paying media and suppliers
Fund third-party costs you pay up front on a client’s behalf, such as media buying or subcontracted work, before you are reimbursed.
Recruitment and contracting
Pay contractors weekly when clients pay monthly or later, a structure invoice finance providers know well.
Taking on a large client
Absorb the cash drag of a client who pays on 60 or 90 day terms without turning down the work.
fit: How the facility works for a firm

The provider advances a share of each approved invoice, often up to around 80 to 90%, and releases the rest, less fees, on payment. As billing grows, the available cash grows. Many firms use it alongside, not instead of, a loan for larger one-off projects.
What providers check

The client list, how concentrated it is, and the payment history of each debtor. Providers prefer a spread of creditworthy business clients, and they may set a limit against any one. They also look at how clean your invoicing is, since disputes over scope or hours can make an invoice ineligible.
Suits invoices, not retained or advance billing

Fees billed in advance or on a retainer collected up front leave nothing to finance. Work on staged fees may only be financeable after each stage is invoiced. Your pattern of billing decides whether the facility is worth the cost.
considerations: Clients may see the arrangement

With factoring, the provider collects payment and clients know. With invoice discounting you collect yourself, which is often discreet. Some professional firms prefer the latter, but providers usually set minimum turnover levels for it.
Fees add up

A service charge and a discount fee apply, with contract minimums and notice periods. Compare the total cost with the benefit of the earlier cash, particularly if your clients mostly pay within thirty days already.
Disputed invoices and recourse
If a client disputes an invoice or refuses to pay, the advance may have to be repaid under a recourse facility. Keep engagement letters and approval records tidy, since the provider may check them.
faqs: Is invoice finance suitable for a small consultancy?

It can be if the firm invoices businesses on credit terms and has a regular ledger. Some providers set a minimum annual turnover, and a very small ledger may not cover fixed charges. A broker can say whether your firm is likely to qualify.
Can I finance only invoices from one large client?

Some providers offer selective facilities for chosen customers or invoices. These can suit a firm with one slow-paying major client, though per-invoice cost may be higher than a full facility. Check how the minimum charges apply. A selective facility can also be a way to test the product before moving the whole ledger across.
Will invoice finance work if I bill by milestone?

It can, once each milestone invoice is raised and approved. The cash is available after invoicing, not before. If most fees are tied to completion certificates or client sign-off, the timing of approval matters more than the payment terms. Your engagement terms and client sign-off process are worth reviewing, because providers may need evidence an invoice is agreed.
How is it different from a revolving credit facility?

Invoice finance borrows against your sales ledger, so the limit grows with billing and relies on client quality. A revolving facility is a fixed limit based on your own accounts. Some firms use one for working capital and the other for specific gaps.
Do I need to give a personal guarantee?

Often, directors are asked for a guarantee in some form, in particular for recourse facilities or for protection against fraud and misuse of funds. The exact requirements vary, so ask the broker what each provider expects. Ask whether any guarantee would be limited to fraud and misuse, or cover unpaid advances too, as the wording differs between providers.

revolving-credit-facility|professional-s.h1: Revolving credit facilities for professional firms
revolving-credit-facility|professional-s.title: Revolving Credit Facilities for Professional Firms | Loanleaf
revolving-credit-facility|professional-s.desc: How a revolving credit facility gives accountants, consultants and agencies a buffer for payroll, tax dates and slow-paying clients, with interest only on use.
revolving-credit-facility|professional-s.lead: A standing credit limit that smooths payroll and tax dates against uneven fee income, repaid as clients pay.
intro: Fee income arrives in clumps, but salaries do not. A firm that bills quarterly, or whose clients settle at the end of an approval process, can look healthy on paper while the account balance dips two days before payroll. A revolving credit facility is a limit you draw on for that dip and repay when the fees arrive. Interest is only charged on what you have drawn, so most of the time the limit sits unused.

It suits firms that are consistently profitable but lumpy: accountancy practices around year-end, architects between design stages, consultancies between project invoices. Lenders will look at bank statements to see that the account normally recovers after each dip. A facility that is drawn and cleared every few weeks is the pattern they want to see, rather than one that stays drawn month after month. A balance that never clears would point towards a term loan instead.
uses: Payroll before fees land
Cover the month-end payroll when a large invoice has been raised but the client has not yet paid.
Tax payment dates
Bridge the days between a VAT or PAYE payment and the client fees that will refill the account.
Counterpart costs before reimbursement
Pay counsel, experts, surveyors or travel on a client’s behalf and recover them on the next invoice.
A buffer around year-end
Hold a reserve to cover a late-paying client or an unexpected delay in a major engagement.
fit: How limits are set

Lenders usually look at annual revenue, profit and the way the bank account behaves. A limit might represent a month or two of costs. For an LLP, lenders also look at members’ drawings. The facility is typically reviewed and renewed annually.
The pattern lenders want to see

A firm that draws, repays and redraws. If bank statements show a steady overdraft that never clears, the lender may suggest a term loan instead, because the need looks structural. Showing that fee income reliably covers the facility is the key point.
Comparing with a bank overdraft

A specialist facility can be arranged separately from your current account, with a defined limit and review date. An overdraft may be cheaper if your bank offers it, but it can be reduced or withdrawn. A broker can compare the two.
considerations: It is not a way to fund growth
Hiring or opening an office needs a term loan, so repayments are planned. Using a revolving facility for long-term investment risks a permanent balance, and a lender can reduce the limit at renewal.
Charges beyond interest
Arrangement, renewal and non-utilisation fees may apply. For a firm that draws occasionally, they can be a large part of the cost. Ask for a worked example based on two or three typical months.
Personal guarantees

Directors or members are often asked to give guarantees. For a firm with few assets, this is common, so understand exactly what you are agreeing to and how it would apply to a partner who later leaves.
faqs: How is it different from invoice finance?

A revolving facility is a fixed limit based on the firm’s own accounts. Invoice finance advances against specific invoices, so the cash available follows your billing. Firms with a few large clients often find invoice finance gives more headroom, while others prefer the simplicity of a limit.
Can I draw on it for any reason?

Usually the limit can be used for general working capital. Some agreements restrict particular uses, so check. Lenders prefer short-term needs that are repaid as fees arrive, rather than long-term spending. The cash available is generally limited to the invoices you have raised, which may suit firms billing regularly in smaller amounts.
Will it affect my bank relationship?

A specialist facility is separate from your main bank, but your bank may see the borrowing on statements, and other lenders will see it on credit files. If a bank loan is planned, mention the facility to the broker. Ask how quickly drawdowns are paid and whether they are available at month end, when payroll pressure is highest.
How long does a facility last?

Terms are usually twelve months, reviewed and renewed at the end, but some lenders offer longer. At review the lender can reduce, change or withdraw the limit, so do not treat it as guaranteed cover. Ask about notice periods, and what the lender would do if your accounts showed a weaker year than the last.
What if my firm is an LLP?

LLPs are eligible if they meet the trading and revenue requirements. Lenders will want to understand how members are paid, how drawings relate to profit and who would give any guarantees. Having the members’ agreement to hand helps. Where profit is shared unevenly, tell the broker so they can explain the position to lenders clearly.

commercial-mortgages|professional-servic.h1: Commercial mortgages for professional services firms
commercial-mortgages|professional-servic.title: Commercial Mortgages for Professional Services Firms | Loanleaf
commercial-mortgages|professional-servic.desc: How a commercial mortgage lets an accountancy, law or architecture firm buy its office, including partner-owned structures, valuation and what lenders check.
commercial-mortgages|professional-servic.lead: Buy the office your firm works from, instead of paying rent, with a mortgage secured on the building.
intro: For a well-established professional firm, a commercial mortgage is a way to stop paying rent to someone else and to hold an asset the firm can later sell, or pass to the next generation of partners. Because the firm’s trading assets are mostly people and relationships, the building is often the only substantial asset on the balance sheet. That can make it attractive to lenders, which see a property they can value and charge.

The buying decision is more than a rent comparison. Fee-earning staff need to be in the right place, and a freehold can limit how the firm adapts if its headcount changes. Many firms buy through a separate property company or a pension scheme, with the practice renting from it. Lenders will want to see the structure, a market rent and the firm’s ability to pay it consistently. Early conversations with a broker can establish which structure lenders are more likely to accept.
uses: Buying the office you rent
Purchase the building the practice already occupies, fixing occupation costs and avoiding rent reviews.
Moving to bigger premises
Buy a larger building as the team grows, sometimes letting part of it to another tenant until you need the space.
A property vehicle owned by the partners
Finance a separate company that owns the office and charges the practice rent, a common structure for partnerships.
Refinancing an existing mortgage
Move to a new lender, change the repayment structure or raise additional capital against the equity in the building.
fit: Deposit and loan to value

Lenders typically lend a proportion of the property’s value, so the firm or its owners need a substantial deposit, often a quarter or more. A professional firm with strong, recurring fee income may be able to borrow at the higher end, though this depends on the lender and the property.
The firm’s income as the real security

For an owner-occupier loan, lenders look at the firm’s profit to see that repayments would be comfortably covered. Where a property company owns the building, they look at the rent the practice pays and at the practice’s accounts as well. Recurring client income helps.
Property type and valuation

A city-centre period building, a converted house or a purpose-built office are valued differently, and lenders consider whether the building could be let to someone else. Offices with flexible layouts and good transport links are generally easier to value.
considerations: Capital tied up in a building

A deposit and the costs of buying use cash that could fund hiring or technology. Weigh the benefit of ownership against what else the money could do, and plan for repairs, insurance and business rates.
Succession and exit

If partners retire, the building must be bought out or sold. A mortgage in the partnership’s name can complicate that, so agree how ownership and borrowing will be handled before you sign. Take legal and tax advice.
Fees and Stamp Duty
Valuation, legal and arrangement fees apply on both sides, plus Stamp Duty Land Tax on a purchase. Some lenders charge early repayment fees, which matter if you might move within a few years.
faqs: Can the partnership or LLP itself take the mortgage?

Often the borrower is a limited company, which may be the firm or a separate property company. LLPs can sometimes borrow directly, though some lenders prefer a company structure. A broker can explain which lenders accept which borrower. Lenders also want clarity on who would sign the mortgage and give any guarantees, so decide this before applying.
Is it better for the partners to own the building personally?

Some prefer to, sometimes through pension arrangements, because it separates the property from the firm’s trading risk. Tax and legal consequences differ, so take specialist advice before choosing. A broker can tell you what lenders will accept. Rent paid to a partner-owned vehicle should be at market level, since lenders check it, and your accountant can advise on tax.
How long can the term be?

Commercial mortgage terms commonly run for fifteen to twenty-five years, and lenders may offer repayment or part-interest structures. A longer term lowers payments but increases the total interest. Match it to how long you expect to hold the building. Some lenders also allow capital repayment holidays or overpayments, so ask about flexibility if fee income varies year to year.
What if I let part of the building to another business?

Rental income can count towards affordability, particularly with a written lease. Lenders may treat the building as part owner-occupied and part investment, and the tenant’s covenant strength may be assessed. Lenders may also ask for a valuation reflecting the building’s alternative uses, so a specialist property or an unusual layout can reduce the amount.
What would stop a lender from lending?

Common issues include a short trading record, heavy dependence on one partner, a small deposit, a building in poor condition or with restricted use, and existing borrowing that reduces affordability. A broker can look at which lenders suit a given case.
